title: Yes means yes
hook: truthfulness in all speech, not just under oath

segments.voice: Yesterday, the little ones: a child set in the middle of the disciples, and a warning about millstones. Your line was protect the little ones. What did you do to keep a child a little safer? Day one thousand two hundred twenty.

"I swear, I'll be there at six." "Honestly, I loved it." "No, seriously, I'll pay you back." Listen to how much extra packaging people wrap around ordinary sentences to make them believable. Swear. Honestly. Seriously. Promise. As if a plain sentence, left on its own, might not be true. Jesus noticed the same habit in his own day, when people swore by heaven, by the earth, by Jerusalem, by their own heads, and quietly treated some oaths as more binding than others. His answer was short. Today: yes means yes.

It's in the Sermon on the Mount. After telling his listeners not to swear at all, Jesus says, in the King James Bible: "But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil." Notice what that does. If you need an oath to be believed, it suggests that your ordinary words are a lower grade of truth. Swearing creates two kinds of speech: the sworn kind you must keep, and the everyday kind you can bend. Jesus folds them back into one. Every word is meant to be the sworn kind. James, writing to early Christians, repeats it almost word for word: "let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay." Christians have applied this in different ways. Quakers, Mennonites and some other churches take it literally and decline to swear oaths, even in court; they make a solemn affirmation instead. Other churches read Jesus as forbidding careless and manipulative oaths, not every oath. They point out that Paul calls God as his witness in his letters, and they allow oaths in court and at ordination. Both sides agree on the heart of it: that the goal is a person whose plain word can be trusted without extra packaging. Yesterday's warning was about not making the little ones stumble. This one is about not making anyone guess. A yes that means yes. A no that means no. And no secret third option hidden behind the words.

Here's the practice: keep your word today. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing you've said you would do that's still hanging: a call you promised, a favor, a deadline, something you told a kid. Hold it plainly. No excuses yet, no reasons. Just the yes you gave. Now picture yourself keeping it, today, in an actual hour of the day. Then notice your words for the rest of the day. Every time you're about to say honestly or I swear, see if the sentence can stand on its own. If you pray, you can offer your words to God. The bell holds the time.
Yes means yes. Jesus's teaching in Matthew 5: let your yea be yea and your nay, nay, so that every plain word is as true as an oath.
Your line: plain truth. Today, keep the one promise you named, and drop the words honestly and I swear. Let your yes be enough. Day one thousand two hundred twenty.

howItsDone: Quakers, Mennonites and some other Christians decline to swear oaths and make a solemn affirmation in court instead; other churches permit oaths for solemn occasions while teaching that all ordinary speech should be truthful.

fork.setup: you're a Quaker called as a witness. the clerk holds out a Bible and asks you to swear. what do you do?
options: make a solemn affirmation instead, and tell the truth.
fork.reveal: Quakers take "swear not at all" literally and affirm instead, where the court allows it. the point isn't to avoid the truth; it's that every word should already be true.

original.note: Greek, Matthew 5:37: yes, yes; no, no.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't lie under oath.
what it means: don't need an oath. let every plain yes and no be as true as a sworn one.
what a scholar hears: James 5:12 echoes Matthew 5:37 so closely that some readers hear the same teaching passed along.
